analysis.one_liner: Lets employers pay a minimum wage raise as health insurance contributions instead of wages.
analysis.headline: Rep. Pete Sessions introduced the bill with zero cosponsors; it was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, never got a vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let employers absorb any federal minimum wage increase by putting an equal amount into each worker's health insurance premium instead of raising the worker's pay — but only for workers the employer already covered [S2][S3]. The worker would see no bigger paycheck; the money Congress intended as wages would go to the insurance plan instead [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to committee, never received a vote, and expired when the Congress ended [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers of minimum-wage workers (in retail, restaurants, and other low-wage industries) would gain the most: instead of paying a mandated raise in cash, they could redirect the same dollars into health premiums they already contribute to, keeping total labor costs flat. Health insurers would also gain premium dollars, since the money would flow into employer-sponsored plans [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: It would have given employers a way to absorb a federal minimum wage increase without raising labor costs: for any covered employee, the employer could increase its health insurance contribution by exactly the amount of the wage increase, and the wage increase would not apply to that employee [S2][S3].

It would have channeled more money into employer-sponsored health insurance, since only employers who already provided coverage — and who raised their premium contribution — could use the offset [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Minimum-wage workers at employers who chose the offset. Their raise would go to the health plan rather than their paycheck, and since the employer already provided coverage, the extra premium dollars would largely offset the employer's own costs — the worker would get cash wages that were no higher [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Workers affected would lose the cash raise Congress intended: the money would go into health insurance premiums instead, and because the employer already provided coverage, the worker might not receive any new benefit in exchange for the smaller paycheck [S2][S3].

The offset was structured so the employer's contribution increase exactly equaled the wage increase, meaning employers who used it would bear no net cost — effectively neutralizing the minimum wage increase for those employees rather than complementing it [S3].
An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill offered nothing to the lowest-paid workers directly; its entire mechanism was to let their employers redirect the raise away from pay [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost outweighed the benefit. The only benefit was flexibility for employers facing a minimum wage increase; the cost was that the workers the minimum wage is meant to help would see smaller paychecks, with the money routed into premiums for coverage they already had. A worker who values cash wages — most minimum-wage workers do — would simply be worse off. The bill died in committee without a vote, so neither cost nor benefit took effect [S1][S5].

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee after referral, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Sessions introduced the bill on November 16, 1999 [S5][S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, the committee with jurisdiction over minimum wage law [S5].
Not a single member of either party cosponsored it [S4].
The committee took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report — and the bill died there when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Minimum-wage workers are better off than they would have been under the bill: the statute that guarantees their wage floor was left intact. Employers of low-wage workers gained nothing, since the offset mechanism they would have used never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Minimum-wage workers kept their wage floor intact

for.name: Rep. Pete Sessions
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 16, 1999, giving employers of already-covered workers an offset against any minimum wage increase

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting the bill expire at the end of the Congress

against.name: Every other member of the House
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors, leaving the bill with no recorded support in either party

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded positions are the Republican sponsor's and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Employers of minimum-wage workers (retail, restaurants, small business)
industries.note: The bill would have let these employers convert a mandated cash raise into a matching health premium contribution, keeping total labor costs flat for any employee they already covered. Its gain came directly out of workers' paychecks.

Money that would otherwise have gone to workers as wages would have been routed into employer-sponsored health premiums instead, increasing premium revenue. Workers would have paid for this in smaller paychecks.
